A small firm, Datasel, received large EU advances despite its limited track record, causing delayed deliveries and alleged substandard shells. Did our AI summary help? At the centre of the controversy is not a major European arms manufacturer, but Datasel SRL, a small Italian company that was acquired by Nagpur-based Neco Defence Munitions. The case raises questions about how Datasel was selected for contracts funded through the European Union’s European Peace Facility, why Estonia paid tens of millions of euros in advance despite the supplier’s limited track record, and what ultimately happened to the ammunition that was supposed to reach Ukraine. Pevkur, who had served as defence minister since 2022, announced that he was prepared to take political responsibility after findings by Estonia’s National Audit Office put the procurement process under scrutiny. “Estonian security is not a one-man project. It is our joint responsibility. That is why I must take political responsibility for the entire defence field today and pass on the baton of the minister of defence to the prime minister at a suitable time,” Pevkur said in a social media post. Russia's intelligence services plotted killings in US, Europe; five charged: FBI How a Ukraine ammunition deal turned into a political crisis According to Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR, the controversy centres on several contracts signed by the Estonian Centre for Defence Investments, or ECDI, with Datasel to procure artillery ammunition for Ukraine. The funding came through the EU’s European Peace Facility, a mechanism used by European countries to support Ukraine and strengthen defence capabilities. The first contract was signed in August 2024. Datasel received an advance payment of €15 million, equivalent to around Rs 164 crore. Two months later, Estonia signed another contract with the company, accompanied by an advance payment of more than €10 million, or approximately Rs 109 crore. Further contracts followed. According to the account of the controversy, the total advance payments eventually reached roughly €70 million, or around Rs 768 crore. The problem was that Datasel did not have an established record of manufacturing the type of artillery ammunition Estonia was seeking. Neither Datasel nor its Indian parent company, Neco Defence Munitions, had previously carried out contracts of this nature, according to ERR. Deliveries were delayed The first ammunition deliveries were expected to reach Ukraine in November 2024. However, the schedule was not met. Deliveries were delayed, and Estonia subsequently alleged that some of the ammunition that did arrive did not meet the required standards. The Estonian government eventually cancelled the contracts. That decision has now become the subject of a legal dispute, with Datasel challenging Estonia’s decision and arguing that it could have fulfilled its contractual obligations had the agreements not been terminated. The controversy therefore involves two competing accounts. Estonia's position centres on delayed deliveries and concerns over the ammunition supplied, while Datasel maintains that the termination was unjustified. The unusual story of Datasel The background of Datasel has become one of the most closely examined aspects of the case. The Italian company was founded in 2005 by businessman Sandro Pazzini. In 2023, the company had only a handful of employees and reported turnover of just over €120,000. Its business profile changed the following year to include wholesale trading in weapons, weapons systems and military ammunition. Datasel was then acquired by Neco Defence Munitions in 2024, with the acquisition completed on March 6, according to the information provided in the reports. That acquisition placed a relatively small Italian company with limited previous experience in the middle of a major European defence procurement involving ammunition for Ukraine. Enter Neco Defence Munitions Neco Defence Munitions is based in Nagpur and is part of Neco Group of Industries. According to information published by the company itself, the group has a turnover of around Rs 7,500 crore. Neco Defence Munitions manufactures a range of ammunition and defence products, including small arms ammunition, large-calibre ammunition, Air Force ammunition and mortar bombs. The company also lists Assam Police, Maharashtra Police and ITC among its major clients. But the specific question in the Estonian case is not whether Neco has experience manufacturing ammunition in general. It is whether Datasel or Neco had the previous experience required to execute the particular artillery ammunition contracts Estonia awarded. According to ERR, neither company had previously undertaken contracts of this kind. Where was the ammunition supposed to come from? Another unresolved issue concerns the actual supply chain. It remains unclear whether Neco Defence Munitions planned to manufacture the ammunition in India or whether Datasel was supposed to procure the shells from another producer and act as an intermediary. That distinction is important because the contracts involved an international supply chain spanning multiple jurisdictions. Datasel itself has pointed to this complexity in defending its performance. In a statement to Euractiv, the company said it had been “the victim” of the dispute and rejected Estonia’s grounds for terminating the contracts. It said it had supplied and invoiced €58 million worth of material against €59 million in advance payments. Datasel also disputed claims surrounding ammunition quality, saying that no quality problems had been established through inspections carried out under the contracts. “The contracts between the parties involved a complex international supply chain and, as is typical for projects of this nature, their execution required multiple approvals, authorisations and clearances involving various governments, regulatory authorities and other stakeholders in different jurisdictions,” the company said. “During the project, certain governmental and regulatory approvals were delayed due to issues and requirements relating to the relevant documentation and approval processes.” Datasel says Estonia’s decision was unjustified The company has also rejected the suggestion that the dispute was primarily about defective ammunition. Speaking to Eesti Ekspress, Datasel said: “Datasel is the party that has suffered losses in connection with these supply contracts. The actions of the Estonian Center for Defence Investments, particularly the reasons given for the extraordinary termination of the contracts, are contradictory and illogical.” The company has acknowledged that delays occurred but maintains that they were connected to regulatory approvals, documentation and the complexity of the international supply chain rather than ammunition quality. Estonia, meanwhile, cancelled the contracts after delays and concerns over the supplies delivered. The dispute is now being fought through legal channels. Why the Indian connection matters The involvement of Neco Defence Munitions has brought an Indian defence company into a controversy that began as an Estonian procurement case. The unusual sequence is central to the story. A relatively small Italian company with limited turnover was acquired by an Indian ammunition manufacturer, after which Datasel became the supplier in contracts worth tens of millions of euros backed by European funds and intended to provide ammunition for Ukraine. Yet, according to ERR, neither Datasel nor its new Indian owner had a previous track record for the specific type of contracts involved. The available accounts also leave unanswered questions about the precise manufacturing and sourcing arrangements behind the ammunition. A procurement dispute with a political fallout For Estonia, the immediate political consequence has been the resignation of its defence minister. Pevkur's decision came after scrutiny of the procurement process and findings by Estonia's National Audit Office. For Datasel, the matter has become a legal and financial dispute over the cancellation of its contracts. And for Neco Defence Munitions, the controversy has placed its international defence business under attention because of its ownership of Datasel and the company's role in the supply chain. The case therefore goes beyond a delayed ammunition shipment. It now involves questions over procurement decisions, advance payments, supplier experience, international approvals and the chain through which European funds intended for Ukraine were converted into ammunition contracts. At the heart of the dispute remains one fundamental question: how did a company with such a limited previous track record in this specific field end up receiving contracts backed by tens of millions of euros in European funding to supply artillery ammunition for Ukraine? Sign up here Martin Belam Mon 28 Sep 2026 07.16 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 07.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Election experts have warned that Donald Trump’s administration could use the crucial hours and days after November’s midterm elections to disrupt the results after struggling to enforce the crackdown it wanted on voting. After a succession of court setbacks to plans to restrict voting access, and with less than six weeks remaining until polls close, the post-election “counting window” is being seen as a particularly vulnerable moment by former US federal government officials. How might Republicans cause doubt over results? Caitlin Durkovich, a former deputy homeland security adviser, said: “I think because the administration has lost so many of their attempts to disrupt the normal process in court, that they are going to use the claim of foreign interference at the end of voting days to either seize equipment or to seize ballots, whether they’re legally justified to do so or not.” What are Democratic prospects for the midterms looking like? With control of the US Congress in the balance, Shrai Popat has interviewed Yasmin Radjy, a grassroots organizer, about what Democrats are getting right – and wrong – in the election run-up . UK counter-terror police investigate Iran link over suspected bomb plot at English base used by US forces View image in fullscreen A B‑1B Lancer bomber parked at RAF Fairford airbase. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters British counter-terrorism police are investigating whether Iran is behind a suspected bomb plot after armed officers found explosives in three vans parked minutes from an RAF base used by the US military. After five men were arrested on terrorism charges, investigators were examining materials found in the vans near RAF Fairford, with an initial view being that they were consistent with improvised explosive devices. What have authorities said about the plot? Counter-terrorism police said: “At around 12.45am Sunday, police received a call relating to three suspicious vehicles which appeared to be travelling towards the airbase. Armed officers responded and five men were arrested.” How did the arrests unfold? A resident of the village of Whelford was driving home from a party when she saw three white vans parked on a country road. She was immediately suspicious , she said, and became all the more so when she spotted a “large group of hooded and balaclavaed” men. She called emergency services and police arrived on the scene 15 minutes later. You can follow the latest developments in this story in our live blog . What has the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, said about attempts to end the US-Iran war? “They were asking for everything upfront with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz told CNN. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.” Republican senator criticizes White House for taxpayer-funded Trump ads View image in fullscreen A screenshot from a pro-Trump ad that the US government paid to broadcast in 2026. Photograph: White House The US senator John Kennedy told CBS News on Sunday “there ought to be a rule” against the White House expanding a taxpayer-funded advertising campaign to promote Donald Trump’s political agenda before the November midterm elections – before tacitly admitting such spending is “probably” illegal. Kennedy appeared to also be acknowledging the argument made by Jamie Raskin, a Democratic congressman, that any government employees who worked on the pro-Trump ads may have committed a felony violation of the Hatch Act, a law that bars government workers from partisan campaign activities. US attorney general defends Trump’s White House media ban View image in fullscreen Todd Blanche, the US attorney general. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters Donald Trump’s attorney general, Todd Blanche, argued that the administration was permitted to ban three news outlets from the White House because “it is a privilege and not a right to be there”. On Thursday, a judge issued a temporary restraining order requiring the White House to temporarily restore the credentials of affected journalists at CNN, MS Now and Politico, and they were allowed entry to the executive complex. However, on Saturday CNN said its journalists were barred from joining the press pool traveling with the president on Air Force One. Pressed to point to a specific report the administration objected to, Blanche seemed to suggest that any negative reporting about Trump must be inaccurate, saying: “The information coming out of CNN and some of these other networks is wholly and completely, almost 100% negative toward the president.” Without providing any evidence, Blanche repeated the administration’s position that the affected three outlets’ reporting amounted to a “national security problem”. In other news … View image in fullscreen Taylor Swift and Madonna. Photograph: CBS/Getty Images Madonna and Taylor Swift triumphed at the 2026 MTV Video Music awards , with the former winning three trophies and the latter winning the night’s top honor, extending her run as the most-awarded artist in VMAs history. Bill Gates has called on the US to regulate the development of artificial intelligence , saying that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths”. Datacenter developers are manipulating the EPA’s air pollution permitting process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental advocates allege. France’s far-right National Rally has surged in senate elections , with Marine Le Pen hailing a “historic victory”. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian The removal of the war debris, in which lives, memories and unexploded Israeli bombs lie buried, is one of largest clearance operations in modern history. Seham Tantesh reports from Gaza City for the Guardian . Composite: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian In New York City activists gathered outside the OpenAI offices during climate week as figures showed that from 2024 to 2026 at least $64bn in proposed datacenter buildout was blocked by local organizing. Photograph: Amber Baeslar for The Washington Post via Getty Images Experts largely attribute the increase in human-bear encounters – up in 15 states – to the impact of unusual weather on the animals’ food sources and a rebound in recent decades in black, brown and grizzly bear populations. … or this: A new museum coaxes Austrians to embrace The Sound of Music View image in fullscreen The Sound of Music featuring Julie Andrews. Photograph: Historical Picture Archive/Alamy It is a beloved classic all over the world – except where it was filmed. Now a new museum aims to lift the profile of The Sound of Music in the beautiful Austrian city of Salzburg, where much of it was made. Climate check: Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii as nor’easter storm batters US east coast View image in fullscreen Cars drive through a flooded road in New Jersey. Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images Hurricane Nolo was moving away from the Hawaiian islands on Sunday , but the threat of heavy rain, flash flooding and strong winds persisted. Mexico’s National Meteorological Service said Polo was expected to make a Baja landfall on Monday. Meanwhile, a nor’easter storm was battering the US east coast with heavy winds causing power outages. Last Thing: Two giant pandas arrive after Xi-Trump summit View image in fullscreen Visitors to Atlanta will soon be able to enjoy sights like this. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images A longstanding diplomatic soft-power move by China has been the loan of endangered giant pandas to zoos, and after Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will be settling in to Atlanta zoo . It is certainly softer diplomacy than the reports that Trump asked Xi if China would like to buy US weapons . The rabbi was a close friend of Pope Francis from their native Argentina. (CNS photo/Paul Haring) (OSV News) — A new Vatican document affirms the Second Vatican Council’s landmark teaching on the Church’s relationship with the Jewish people and those of other faiths, while inviting humanity to enter upon a common “journey of hope.” That journey requires “courage” and “a genuine shift in mindset” to seek “peaceful coexistence” amid “unprecedented challenges,” including conflicts, persecution, the weaponization of religion, secularization and polarization, said the document. And rather than looking to found “one great world religion,” authentic interreligious dialogue aims to build “a fraternal society capable of accepting differences,” said the text. On Sept. 16, the Vatican released “A Journey of Hope: Sixty Years of Interreligious Dialogue and Fraternity in the Light of the Conciliar Declaration ‘Nostra Aetate.’” The 8,600-word note was the result of a collaboration among the Vatican’s Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity — which also oversees religious relations with Judaism — and the Dicastery for Interreligious Dialogue. Pope Leo XIV had granted approval of the text on June 22, with official publication taking place Sept. 16. Pope Leo XIV greets Silviu Vexler, president of the Federation of Jewish Communities in Romania, during a ceremony honoring Blessed Iuliu Hossu in the Sistine Chapel at the Vatican June 2, 2025. (CNS photo/Vatican Media) The five-part “Journey of Hope” began by retracing the “essential stages” in the Church’s interreligious dialogue since the 1965 promulgation of “Nostra Aetate,” including the contributions of Pope Leo XIV and his four predecessors. The note then examined the “visible” and “silent” fruits of “Nostra Aetate,” as well as the “persistent resistance and misunderstandings” that surround the conciliar document. In their note, the three dicasteries called for a renewed “pedagogy of dialogue,” one that puts into practice an informed encounter between Catholics and those of other beliefs. A ‘profound change’ in response to the Shoah The note recapped the development and promulgation of “Nostra Aetate,” which “marked a profound change” in how the Church both understood and expressed its relationship with those of other faiths. The dicasteries said “Nostra Aetate” aligned with another conciliar document, “Dignitatis Humanae,” which declared religious freedom a human right. Specifically, said the note, “Nostra Aetate” was conceived as the Church’s response to the Shoah, the preferred Hebrew term for the systematic, state-sponsored persecution and murder of six million European Jews from 1933-1945 by the German Nazi regime, its allies and collaborators. Pope Leo XIV speaks to representatives of the Romanian Greek Catholic Church and Romania’s Jewish community during a ceremony honoring Blessed Iuliu Hossu in the Sistine Chapel at the Vatican June 2, 2025. (CNS photo/Vatican Media) The note recalled a pivotal meeting between St. John XXIII and French academic Jules Isaac, who lost his wife, daughter and son-in-law at Auschwitz, and who had published a study of the Church’s long-running “teaching of contempt” regarding Judaism and Jews. That encounter, dated by scholars to June 13, 1960, is considered a major catalyst for the drafting of “Nostra Aetate.” The dicasteries said in their note that “official and institutional Catholic-Jewish dialogue finds its foundation” in “Nostra Aetate,” which is also “the first magisterial statement that clearly recognizes the Jewish roots of Christianity.” “Nostra Aetate” — the tenets of which have been upheld and expounded upon by successive popes — illuminated the “fundamental principle” that “respect and esteem” must undergird interreligious dialogue, said the dicasteries. A unique dialogue based on a ‘rich, shared heritage’ The note highlighted the “distinctive character” of Jewish-Christian dialogue, given the “rich shared heritage” the two faith traditions share. “What Jesus brought into Christianity, as a Jewish inheritance, forms part of the theological structure of Christianity itself,” said the note. The dicasteries stressed that Jewish-Christian dialogue cannot be regarded as “secondary,” but as “a matter of becoming fully aware of one’s own original identity.” Citing Church teaching, the note observed that “God’s covenant with the Jewish people is irrevocable,” something that “continually challenges the Church.” That reality “does not mean, for Christians, that there are two paths to salvation or that the covenant with the Jewish people runs parallel to the Christian way of salvation,” said the note, stating that “the Church teaches that Christ is the one and only Redeemer.” Still, the “irrevocable covenant has theological significance,” said the note, adding that “the more Christians come to know and love the Jewish roots of their own tradition, the better they understand themselves in the practice of faith, and the stronger their religious identity becomes.” Dialogue continues amid modern conflicts The note emphasized that “the religious life of contemporary Jews” is also “relevant to Christians.” Such “solidarity with the Jewish people also includes the shared struggle against antisemitism,” said the dicasteries. The note admitted that “the conflicts that have erupted in the Middle East in recent years” have “left their mark on Jewish-Christian dialogue,” straining “many channels of communication.” Pope Leo XIV and Rector of the Great Mosque of Algiers Mohammed Al-Mamoun Al-Qasimi Al-Hassani during a visit to the Great Mosque of Algiers (Djamaa El Djazair), in Mohamadia, Algiers, Algeria, April 13, 2026. (OSV News photo/Guglielmo Mangiapane, Reuters) Those channels “continue to be tested by differing interpretations of the events that have unfolded, interpretations that are often not unanimous even within the respective religious communities,” said the dicasteries. Nonetheless, “the pillars of dialogue among believers, built over sixty years of common effort, have remained firm,” the note said. Citing St. John Paul II, the dicasteries emphasized that dialogue with other religious traditions is “part of the Church’s evangelizing mission.” Fruits of friendship in everyday life The dicasteries said that six decades after its promulgation, “Nostra Aetate” has borne fruit in the Church’s relations with Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and numerous faith traditions, including traditional religions. The note pointed to the postconciliar flourishing of “enduring friendships” among religious leaders, “joint educational and social projects” and collaborative responses to humanitarian needs, conflict and environmental crises. Such fruits “are often lived out quietly and discreetly, rooted in everyday life” by “priests, religious, and the lay faithful,” said the dicasteries. These results, said the note, “embody the intuition of ‘Nostra Aetate’: to live in the world as witnesses to the love of God, in dialogue with all.” The dicasteries expressed hope such dialogue could extend to “members of ‘new religious movements’ and representatives of new religious experiences.” Such “fraternal encounters,” while not ecumenical or interreligious dialogue “properly speaking,” can provide chances to work together around “shared values” and the “common good,” said the note, stressing the need for “clarity about one’s own identity” and “mutual respect.” The dicasteries also said another fruit of “Nostra Aetate” was “the growing critical awareness of manifestations of Islamophobia.” “Contemporary challenges” demand a “genuine shift in mindset,” including a renewed approach to dialogue itself based on greater religious literacy as well as an authentic commitment to peace, flexibility and friendship, said the note. “This journey of hope remains open, and all of us are invited to walk it together with courage,” said the dicasteries.
